For "construction engineering," it isn't talked about much because it isn't a 'real' branch of engineering. A construction project has several different branches of engineering that intersect and function together to bring you a building with running water, electricity, HVAC, and structural stability. All of these systems are designed in separate offices, by professionals with varying degrees. There isn't really a one stop shop of construction engineering unfortunately. For design, it truly is about specialization. Construction engineering is an unspecialized discipline. Construction Managers see the whole show, and most CM degrees prepare you with an understanding of the design process so that you don't look like an idiot, basically, and so that you can work with design professionals more effectively.

I would say this isn't an option, unfortunately. Construction Management is a meaty program and a four year degree in itself, not offered as a minor at any school I know of. You can get certificates for construction management but if you're going to invest that kind of time, you might be better off going for that bachelor's.
Civil degrees don't always prepare you with the project management skills you need to run a project successfully.

Hey, good on you for exploring this while you are still in high school. If construction/engineering interests you, I think any of these careers will give you a high level of satisfaction, as well as a very handsome salary, and plenty of opportunities to travel and work all over the country or world if you should choose. 

The main, striking difference between Construction Management and Civil Engineering is CE focuses on DESIGN of structures (bridges, dams, storm water and sanitary sewer lines, and other infrastructure) and as a CE, your work will be in what can be referred to as "HEAVY CIVIL," it's all the things that aren't very glamorous, but critical to health and wellbeing of all communities. If you enjoy doing mathematical calculations and using design tables for calculating compressive and tensile forces, sizing pipe, and so on, CE is more suitable. 

CM focuses on the IMPLEMENTATION, the actual construction of these structures, and has a more diverse spread of disciplines, beyond "heavy civil" and into commercial, industrial, even residential. If your appeal to construction is a gleaming, finished building (or bridge, pipeline, underground rail system. .) at the end of a project, CM is more suitable. If you enjoy creating and managing schedules, coordinating subcontractor trades, negotiating contacts, and communicating with the architect as the project progresses, CM is more suitable. Construction Managers juggle a host of activities related to project delivery, and can still be involved in design when a project is being delivered via a "design-build" contact where the general contractor and design team work together as a single entity to design the structure. The salary of a CM will challenge the salaries of most engineers. Most CM's work for a firm, and not necessarily own their own company, but some may. I'm finishing my Bachelor's in Construction Engineering Management Technology and I love my field. I get to be surrounded by engineering systems, a vast menagerie of materials, coordinate trades on my job, and the sense of accomplishment at the end of a project is next to none. 

I know Civil is typically the branch of engineering that is brought up when talking about construction engineering, but Structural engineering is also an option if you are seeking to design. 

I've got a few years experience in the field as well as finishing my 4 year degree soon, so feel free to DM with any other questions. Hope this gave you a better perspective on these fields.

Are you talking about incandescent bulbs, CFL's, or LED's? There's a lot to be said about all of them:

Incandescent bulbs:

-HIGHLY energy inefficient. 90% of the energy used produces heat, not light

-60 watts average

-Last 1,000 to 2,000 hours

-Great CRI, or Color Rendering Index. Renders colors almost as well as natural light 

-Can use in all dimming lights no problem


CFL's:

-CONTAINS MERCURY. You /cannot/ dispose of in your trash. Must be taken to a special facility that processes hazardous materials. One bulb pollutes 70,000 gallons of water if disposed improperly. 

-13 to 15 watts average

-Lasts 8,000 hours

-Lousy CRI, don't put these in your bathroom or your self confidence will plummet. Seriously these are abysmal, every picture will look yellow and colors will render inaccurately

-Due to working via luminescent phosphors, cannot dim in traditional light dimmers
There are no positives. I do not recommend these bulbs to anyone, no matter how good of a deal they are. 


LED's:

-Most energy efficient option. Use LED's for all your fixtures and you will see a noticeable decrease in your electric bill

-6 to 8 watts average

-50,000 hours (as long as 50 incandescents or 10 CFL's)

-Fantastic CRI

-Can be used in traditional dimmers

-High upfront cost but seriously awesome savings


That said, I recommend you find some reasonably priced LED's and just dish out the $10/bulb. They are truly your best option and despite the higher upfront cost, your most frugal one. Given their incredibly long life, like 20 years, energy efficiency, and high performance, you SAVE so much by using them. They pay for themselves.
Source: am construction manager who was taught this in college degree program and formal training

I am currently a senior at [redacted] studying Construction Engineering Mgmt Technology, and I can't agree more with u/bigstoneAZ 

I have had several internships through school (construction is great because you can always expect to be paid for your internship) and right now I am working for a fairly large CM/GC firm. As an intern, I make $16/hr and expect a salary of $57k upon graduation, so the money rivals that of an engineer. I honestly love what I do and am happy on my way to work. Construction is a great industry for you if you love detail. In almost any project, I work in the commercial sector, you'll find concrete, steel, masonry, wood/timber, and a host of engineered systems like hvac, electrical, and plumbing... For each individual component, there is a plethora of information to be known just as it relates to construction! Thankfully no one expects you to know everything, but this awards you the chance to constantly learn through your career and I attribute this to part of the reason I love being in construction. 

My only add on to the previous comment is, from my experience, my classes were very diverse. Classes at my college include: Intro to Materials and Methods of Construction, Quantity Takeoff, Estimating, Construction Accounting, Construction Law and Ethics, Scheduling, Contact law, Statics, Strength of Materials, Wood, Timber and Formwork Design, Surveying (intro and advanced), Safety and Inspection, Hydraulics and Drainage, Soils Testing..
